799.title: Which voice speaks to you
799.hook: each reader finds one Bhagat who feels like a friend
799.howItsDone: Sikhs read and sing the Bhagats' hymns as part of the Guru, and some readers return again and again to particular shabads, including Bhagats' hymns, that they hold dear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ang: one Bhagat a morning, the page number as the address, and your line, one a day. Today, a question about those voices.

Which of these voices would you sit next to on a long bus ride? Not which one is greatest. The Granth doesn't rank them, and neither will i. Just which one you'd want beside you. The one who asks plainly for flour and a cow. The one who dreams of a city with no sorrow in it. The one who says hard things with a grin. Some readers find, after a while, one voice they keep going back to.
screen: `A LONG BUS RIDE.` → `NOT WHO'S GREATEST.` → `WHO YOU'D SIT BESIDE.`

segments.voice: Listen to how differently they speak. Dhanna, the farmer, in Raag Dhanasri on Ang 695, makes an arti, a hymn of worship, that reads in paraphrase like a shopping list handed to God: flour, lentils, a little ghee, shoes, good clothes, a cow, a horse. A man asking his Lord for what a household needs, without embarrassment. Ravidas, in Raag Gauri on Ang 345, describes Begampura, the place without sorrow: no tax, no fear, no one second or third class. That city, he says, is his home. Kabir, in his saloks, is the friend who tells you the truth to your face and doesn't soften it, often with a picture from the loom or the market. And Farid, in Raag Asa on Ang 488, sings of hearts dyed in love for God, verses that ache for the Beloved. A farmer's frankness. A dream of a fair city. A sharp tongue. A long ache. All in one book, all sung as gurbani, none placed above another. So the question isn't which one is right. It's which one you can hear. Someone in a hard month might lean toward Farid. Someone tired of a world that sorts people might lean toward Ravidas. Someone who prays best in plain words might lean toward Dhanna. Gurbani speaks of the Lord as a friend, mit or sajan. A favorite Bhagat doesn't replace that. It's more like a friend who shows the way to the Friend.
screen: `DHANNA ASKS FOR FLOUR AND A COW.` · `RAVIDAS DREAMS OF A CITY WITHOUT SORROW.` · `KABIR AND FARID: SHARP TONGUE, LONG ACHE.` · `NONE RANKED; WHICH ONE CAN YOU HEAR?` · then, large: `A FRIEND IN THE GRANTH.`

segments.voice: Let the four voices pass by, one at a time: Dhanna's plain list, Ravidas's city, Kabir's sharp line, Farid's ache. Don't choose too fast; just notice which one you'd want to hear again tomorrow, and if none stands out, that's an answer too, and the week of reading will help. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Mit. Gurbani's word for a friend: the Lord as a friend, and a favorite Bhagat as a friend who shows the way to the Friend.
Your line: a friend in the granth. No ranking, just a voice you can hear. Seven hundred ninety-nine days, and counting.

800.title: One Guru, many voices
800.hook: Sikhs honor the Bhagats' hymns as fully part of the Guru
800.howItsDone: Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib as the living Guru, opening it each morning and laying it to rest each evening, and every hymn in it, the Gurus' and the Bhagats', is honored in the same way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mit: Dhanna's plain list, Ravidas's city, Kabir's edge, Farid's ache, and your line, a friend in the granth. Today, the book they all share.

Someone walks into the gurdwara hall, takes off their shoes, covers their head, and walks up the aisle toward the Granth under its canopy. They kneel and touch their forehead to the floor. A small question hides in that bow: which part of the book is it for? The Gurus' hymns? The pages of Kabir, the pages of Farid, the minstrels' Var? Nobody bows to a chapter. The bow goes to the whole Granth at once.
screen: `SHOES OFF, HEAD COVERED.` → `A BOW TO THE FLOOR.` → `WHICH PAGES IS IT FOR?`

segments.voice: Sikhs call the Granth the Guru Granth Sahib, and they mean Guru: not a book about the Guru, but the Guru present, honored as a living teacher. Sikhs say Guru Gobind Singh passed the guruship to the Granth, and since then there has been no human Guru. Now count the voices in it. The Gurus wrote under one name: their hymns carry the signature Nanak, whether the hymn is by Guru Nanak or Guru Arjan or another Guru, and a heading marked Mahala tells you which. Many hands, one name. Then the Bhagats, from different trades and towns and paths, with their own names in the headings. Then the Bhatts' swayyas, the minstrels' Var, Sundar's Sadd. Different voices from different times and places, some from Hindu backgrounds, some Muslim. Sikhs don't treat these as layers of lesser and greater. Guru Ram Das, in Raag Nat on Ang 982, says in paraphrase that the bani is the Guru and the Guru is the bani. The word itself is the teacher. That line is the key to this whole block. If the word is the Guru, then every word in the Guru's book is the Guru's word, whoever's mouth it first came from. Kabir's line and Guru Nanak's get the same canopy, the same chauri waved over them, the same morning opening and evening rest. Not one voice: one Guru speaking through many voices.
screen: `THE GRANTH IS THE GURU, PRESENT.` · `THE GURUS SIGN AS NANAK.` · `BHAGATS, BHATTS, MINSTRELS: MANY VOICES.` · `THE BANI IS THE GURU.` · then, large: `ONE GURU.`

segments.voice: Picture the whole book closed under its cloth, every voice inside it: the Gurus, the Bhagats, the minstrels. If you're near a gurdwara or a Granth today, you can let one bow carry all of it in mind; for now, breathe with the picture, with Waheguru on each breath out if you pray, and lower your head slightly at the end, a small bow.

Your line: one bow covers them all. Many voices, and one teacher for them all. Day eight hundred.

801.title: The Bhagats close
801.hook: the Guru's book is a house with room for saints of every kind
801.howItsDone: Sikhs read and sing the Bhagats' hymns as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs point to them, along with langar and the shared sangat, as the Guru's teaching that the door is open to people of every caste and faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one Guru: the bani is the Guru, and your line, one bow covers them all. Today, the Bhagats' block closes.

A big family dinner, and the extra chairs keep coming out of the back room. A cousin's new husband. A neighbor nobody expected. The aunt who isn't speaking to the uncle, seated three chairs away from him. Somehow the table stretches, and nobody is sent home to eat alone. For a long stretch now, you and i have been walking through a book that works like that table. Today the question is simple: who got a chair?
screen: `A LONG FAMILY TABLE.` → `MORE CHAIRS FROM THE BACK.` → `WHO GOT A CHAIR?`

segments.voice: Look down the table. Kabir, the weaver of Benares, with his warp and weft and his sharp tongue. Sheikh Farid of Pakpattan, a Sufi, asking you to look under your own collar. Namdev, the calico printer, whose temple, tradition says, turned to face him. Ravidas, the shoemaker, whose family carried the dead cattle, dreaming of Begampura. Then the others. Trilochan and the last thought. Beni and the stages of life. Dhanna the farmer. Sain the barber. Pipa the king. Sadhna's plea for grace. Ramanand's home colored with love. Parmanand: hear, then do. Surdas's single line. Jaidev, the old poet. Bhikhan's medicine. And around them, the Bhatts with their praise, Satta and Balvand forgiven and sung, the saloks to Mardana, Sundar's call. A weaver beside a king. A Muslim saint beside a Hindu devotee. A man from a family others kept at a distance beside a Brahmin. Guru Arjan, in Raag Suhi on Ang 747, says in paraphrase that the teaching is shared by all four castes, the Khatri, the Brahmin, the Shudra and the Vaishya alike. The Bhagat pages put that line into practice: the Gurus didn't just say the table was open, they set the places. And the room wasn't made by agreeing on everything. The Gurus kept voices they answered, sometimes putting the same image another way. The table holds difference without throwing anyone out. Tomorrow the path turns from the book to the people around the Gurus, starting at home, with Guru Nanak's mother and father.
screen: `WEAVER, SUFI, CALICO PRINTER, SHOEMAKER.` · `FARMER, BARBER, KING, AND MORE.` · `ONE TEACHING FOR ALL FOUR CASTES.` · `ROOM WITHOUT AGREEING ON EVERYTHING.` · then, large: `ROOM FOR ALL.`

Sant. A saint or holy person: the weaver, the Sufi, the shoemaker, the farmer, the barber and the king, all honored this way at one table.
Your line: room for all. The table stretches, and nobody eats alone. That's day eight hundred one.

802.title: Mata Tripta and Mehta Kalu
802.hook: Nanak's mother loved him gently; his father, an accountant, worried for his future
802.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the stories of Guru Nanak's childhood from the janamsakhis, especially at Gurpurab, and the sacha sauda, the true bargain, is among the stories children hear at home and in gurdwara classes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sant: a weaver beside a king, a Sufi beside a shoemaker, and your line, room for all. Today, the path walks into a home.

A father counts coins into his son's hand. Go to the market, he says. Buy well, sell well, come home with a profit. The son comes home with empty hands and no goods. On the road, he says, he met holy men who hadn't eaten, and he fed them. That was the true bargain. The father is furious. The mother, as tradition remembers her, is gentler. A new part of the path begins today: the people around the Gurus, starting at home, with Mata Tripta and Mehta Kalu.
screen: `COINS FOR THE MARKET.` → `EMPTY HANDS, FED STRANGERS.` → `A NEW PART: THE PEOPLE AROUND THE GURUS.`

segments.voice: The story of the coins isn't in the Granth. It comes from the janamsakhis, the old life-stories of Guru Nanak, and Sikhs remember it as the sacha sauda, the true bargain. The janamsakhis sketch his parents in a few strokes. His father, Mehta Kalu, kept the village accounts: a practical man with a practical hope, that his son would find steady work and get on in the world. His mother, Mata Tripta, the stories remember as gentle, the one who loved the boy as he was. The stories don't make Mehta Kalu a villain. A father worried about money and a future isn't a bad man. He's a father. In one story the boy grows quiet and withdrawn, lying for days without wanting to eat, and the worried family calls in a physician. Here the Granth itself has a line. In a salok in Raag Malar, on Ang 1279, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: they called the physician to treat me; he took my arm and felt for the illness; the simple physician doesn't know the pain is deep inside, in the heart. Whether that salok was spoken in that very room, the sources don't settle. But it fits. The family's worry was real, and so was their love. They just couldn't see where the ache was. Neither parent fully understood their son, and both of them loved him. Love and worry live in the same house, often in the same parent.
screen: `THE TRUE BARGAIN: A JANAMSAKHI STORY.` · `A FATHER WHO KEPT ACCOUNTS.` · `A PHYSICIAN WHO MISSED THE ACHE.` · `GENTLENESS AND WORRY, BOTH LOVE.` · then, large: `LOVE AND WORRY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who worried about you, a parent, a grandparent, a guardian, an older friend, and one thing they worried over, maybe something that annoyed you at the time. Look underneath it for the love that was holding it; you don't have to agree with the worry, just see what it was made of. If you pray, let Waheguru come with each breath out.
Mata. A title of honor for the Gurus' mothers and wives: Guru Nanak's mother, gentle, her husband worried, and love and worry living in the same home.
Your line: love and worry. One house, often one parent, holds them both. See you tomorrow.

803.title: Bebe Nanaki and Jai Ram
803.hook: his sister and her husband took Nanak to Sultanpur and found him work
803.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Bebe Nanaki in the stories of Guru Nanak's life, and the tera, tera story from the Sultanpur storehouse is told to children as a lesson that everything belongs to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Tripta and Mehta Kalu: a mother's gentleness, a father's worry, and your line, love and worry. Today, the sister.

Back home, things aren't going well. The young man gives away what he's meant to sell. He sits for hours with wandering holy men. His father is running out of patience. Then a message comes from another town. His older sister has married and moved away, and she and her husband have a room, and maybe a job. Come stay with us, she says.
screen: `THINGS AREN'T GOING WELL AT HOME.` → `A MESSAGE FROM ANOTHER TOWN.` → `COME STAY WITH US.`

segments.voice: Bebe Nanaki was Guru Nanak's older sister. Bebe is an affectionate word for an elder sister, and Sikhs still say her name with it. In the janamsakhis, she's the one in the family who seems to see her brother clearly from the start: where others saw a boy who wouldn't settle, the stories have her seeing something holy. She married Jai Ram, who, tradition says, worked in Sultanpur for the local governor, Daulat Khan Lodi. And here help becomes practical. Jai Ram used his place to find his wife's brother a job in the modikhana, the government storehouse where grain was kept and given out. Not a glamorous detail: a brother-in-law making a call. The stories say Nanak did the work honestly and well. And they tell one famous moment from that storehouse. Weighing out grain, counting each measure aloud, he came to the number tera, which in Punjabi also means yours. Tradition says he stopped counting and kept saying it: tera, tera, yours, yours, everything is Yours. It was in Sultanpur, too, in the stories, that his great turning came. But notice who got him there. Not a king or a priest. A sister who believed in him, and a brother-in-law who opened a door. Family who helps doesn't always look like a sermon. Sometimes it's a spare room and an introduction.

804.title: Mata Sulakhni
804.hook: Nanak's wife, whose steadiness made the travels possible
804.tomorrow: Mata Khivi, named in the Granth
804.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Mata Sulakhni as Guru Nanak's wife and the mother of Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das, and her place in his life is remembered in the tellings of his marriage and travels.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bebe Nanaki and Jai Ram: a sister who believed and a door opened in Sultanpur, and your line, family who helps. Today, the one who stayed home.

Behind a famous journey there's often someone who didn't go. Someone who kept the lamps lit, answered the door, fed the children, and was there when the traveler came back dusty from the road. The traveler gets the stories. The one at home gets a line or two, if that. The janamsakhis tell and retell Guru Nanak's long journeys. The woman who stayed is mentioned far more briefly. Today, her name: Mata Sulakhni.
screen: `SOMEONE WHO DIDN'T GO.` → `THE TRAVELER GETS THE STORIES.` → `A LINE OR TWO FOR HOME.`

segments.voice: Start with honesty about the sources. The janamsakhis say much more about Guru Nanak's travels than about his marriage. Mata Sulakhni appears in them, but she rarely speaks. Tradition says she was the daughter of Mool Chand and that they married at Batala. Their sons were Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das. Beyond that, the old stories give us her presence more than her words, and it would be wrong to fill the silence with made-up speeches. So look at what they do show. When Guru Nanak left on his long journeys, preaching the Name far from home, someone had to keep that home standing: the children raised, the household run. That was Mata Sulakhni, and in some tellings the family, including Bebe Nanaki, helped her. Without that steadiness, the travels don't happen. Nobody can carry a message across many lands if the ground behind them is falling apart. A great deal of faithful life looks like this. Not a sermon from a mountaintop. A pot on the stove, a child's lesson checked, a door answered, day after day, while someone else's work goes out into the world. Sikhs call her Mata, mother, as a title of honor. Steady at home isn't the small part of the story. It's the part the rest of the story stands on.

805.title: Mata Khivi, named in the Granth
805.hook: Guru Angad's wife is praised by name in the minstrels' Var for her generous kitchen (Ramkali, ang 967)
805.howItsDone: Gurdwaras run a langar, a free kitchen where anyone may sit and eat, and Sikhs remember Mata Khivi as one who shaped that service at Khadur Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Sulakhni kept the home standing while Guru Nanak traveled; your line was steady at home. Today, a kitchen, and a name in scripture.

A huge pot of rice pudding, thick and sweet, a ladle as long as a forearm, and a line of people that doesn't end. Somebody has to decide the pudding gets real ghee, not the cheap stuff, even with so many mouths. That somebody, in the Guru's house at Khadur, has a name, and the name made it into scripture. It's also the end of a week, so there's a look back too.
screen: `A HUGE POT OF RICE PUDDING.` → `REAL GHEE, FOR EVERYONE.` → `A NAME IN SCRIPTURE.`

segments.voice: Mata Khivi was the wife of Guru Angad, and Sikhs remember her as the one who ran the langar, the free kitchen, at Khadur. Some people in this part of the path are known mainly from later stories, like the janamsakhis. Mata Khivi is named in the Granth itself. Remember Satta and Balvand, the minstrels whose Var sits in Raag Ramkali? On Ang 967, Balvand speaks of her. In paraphrase: Khivi is a good woman, and her shade is thick and cool, like a leafy tree. In the langar, the wealth of the Word is shared out, and rice pudding made with ghee is served, sweet as nectar. Two kinds of food in one line: the Word, given freely, and kheer, rice pudding rich with ghee, given just as freely. Shade is the picture: people come in from the heat and rest under her care. A woman's kitchen work is honored in the Guru's book, by name, as part of the Guru's house. The langar isn't a side room to the faith; it's where the faith gets fed to people. And the generosity is in the ghee. Feeding many people cheaply would have been easier. The line praises richness. Now the week: which voice speaks to you. One Guru, many voices. The Bhagats close, with room for all. Then home: Mata Tripta and Mehta Kalu, love and worry. Bebe Nanaki and Jai Ram, family who helps. Mata Sulakhni, steady at home. And today, Mata Khivi's generous kitchen.
screen: `MATA KHIVI RAN THE LANGAR.` · `NAMED IN THE VAR, ANG 967.` · `SHADE LIKE A LEAFY TREE; KHEER WITH GHEE.` · `A WEEK OF VOICES AND A HOME.` · then, large: `GENEROUS KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: Picture a meal you'll make or share this week, and who could eat it with you. Then picture the ghee: the one thing you could make a little richer than you have to, more of something good, a second helping set aside, a neighbor's plate. If you pray, you can breathe Waheguru out with it.
